extracted.intended_audience: upper-level undergraduate and beginning graduate students learning algebraic geometry
extracted.subtask_description: Expository textbook material giving definitions, examples, and theorems about Hilbert functions/polynomials, degrees and Bézout's theorem, and the basic theory of morphisms, presheaves, sheaves, stalks and germs for affine/projective/quasi-projective varieties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hilbert function of a double point (example)
rubrics_metrics.description: For the 'double point' ideal I = (x^2, y) in C[x,y,z], the graded quotient decomposes and one deduces h_I(d) = 2 for d = 1,2,3,... and h_I(0) = 1.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This example illustrates how non-reduced schemes can contribute multiplicity to the Hilbert function; the computation uses the decomposition C[x,y,z]/(x^2,y) ≅ C[z] ⊕ xC[z].

rubrics_metrics.name: Hilbert function equality for different schemes (example)
rubrics_metrics.description: The coordinate ring C[x,y,z]/(x^2−z^2, y−z) ≅ C[z] ⊕ xC[z], so a reducible variety consisting of two reduced points can have the same Hilbert function as the double point example above.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Shows that Hilbert function alone does not distinguish reduced vs non-reduced structure; the same Hilbert function can arise from different ideals/ring structures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hilbert functions for empty/projectively irrelevant ideal
rubrics_metrics.description: If I ⊊ C[x0,...,xn] has V_pr(I) = ∅ (e.g. I contains a power of each xi so that I contains the irrelevant ideal (x0,...,xn)), then h_I(d) = 0 for all sufficiently large d (notation: h_I(d)=0 for d ≫ 0).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This captures the behavior of Hilbert functions for ideals with empty projective variety; the irrelevant ideal annihilates all large-degree components.

rubrics_metrics.name: Additivity relation for Hilbert functions (Proposition 80.2.7)
rubrics_metrics.description: For homogeneous ideals I and J in C[x0,...,xn], the Hilbert functions satisfy h_{I∩J} + h_{I+J} = h_I + h_J (as functions of degree d).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof uses a short exact sequence of graded pieces 0 → [S/(I∩J)]_d → [S/I]_d ⊕ [S/J]_d → [S/(I+J)]_d → 0 and finite-dimensional vector-space dimensions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hilbert function of a finite set of projective points (Theorem 80.2.9)
rubrics_metrics.description: If V is a projective variety consisting of m points (m ≥ 0), then h_V(d) = m for all sufficiently large d (h_V(d) = m for d ≫ 0).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof by induction on m using the additivity proposition and the fact that ideals whose projective variety is empty have vanishing Hilbert function in large degree.

rubrics_metrics.name: Eventual constancy for zero-dimensional projective varieties (Corollary 80.2.11)
rubrics_metrics.description: If I is an ideal with V_pr(I) finite (dimension 0), then the Hilbert function h_I is eventually constant (stabilizes to the total number of points counted with multiplicity).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follows by induction and previous examples/theorems; applies regardless of whether the ideal is radical.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hilbert function of projective space CP^n (Example 80.3.1)
rubrics_metrics.description: h_{CP^n}(d) = binomial(d+n, n) = (d+n)(d+n−1)...(d+1)/n!, a polynomial in d of degree n.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This 'balls and urns' combinatorial count shows Hilbert functions can be polynomial in d and identifies the polynomial for projective space.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hilbert function of the parabola (Example 80.3.2)
rubrics_metrics.description: For the parabola zy − x^2 in CP^2, the graded quotient decomposes giving h_{(zy−x^2)}(d) = 2d − 1 (e.g., values at small d: 1,3,5...).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Combinatorial counting of basis monomials modulo the relation zy = x^2 yields the linear polynomial in d; illustrates eventual polynomial behavior in a concrete curve example.

rubrics_metrics.name: Existence and properties of the Hilbert polynomial (Theorem 80.3.3)
rubrics_metrics.description: (a) For any homogeneous ideal I ⊆ C[x0,...,xn] there exists a polynomial χ_I such that h_I(d) = χ_I(d) for all sufficiently large d. (b) deg χ_I = dim V_pr(I) (with χ_I = 0 if V_pr(I)=∅). (c) m! · χ_I has integer coefficients (where m = deg χ_I).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof by induction on dimension using hyperplane section and a finite-difference identity: h_I(d) − h_I(d−1) = h_{I+(x0)}(d). This theorem formalizes 'eventually polynomial' behavior of Hilbert functions and links degree of the polynomial to geometric dimension.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of Hilbert polynomial and degree of an ideal (Definition 80.4.1)
rubrics_metrics.description: χ_I is called the Hilbert polynomial of I. If χ_I is nonzero, the (geometric) degree of I is defined as the leading coefficient of m!·χ_I and denoted deg I.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For projective varieties V one sets h_V = h_{I_rad(V)} and deg V = deg I_rad(V). Note remark that degree of ideal is distinct from degree of Hilbert function as a polynomial expression.

rubrics_metrics.name: Basic properties of degree (Proposition 80.4.3)
rubrics_metrics.description: If V and W are varieties of the same dimension and disjoint then deg(V ∪ W) = deg V + deg W. If dim V < dim W then deg(V ∪ W) = deg W.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Degree is additive across components of maximal dimension and measures the 'degree' of the highest-dimensional component; follows from properties of Hilbert polynomial and additivity of Hilbert functions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examples of degrees (Example 80.4.4)
rubrics_metrics.description: Illustrative list: (a) finite set of n points has degree n; (b) a double point has degree 2; (c) CP^n has degree 1; (d) any line or plane (isomorphic to CP^1 or CP^2) has degree 1; (e) the parabola has degree 2; (f) union of parabola and a point has degree 2.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Helps build intuition: degree corresponds to geometric notion (e.g., curve of degree k intersects hyperplane in k points counting multiplicity).

rubrics_metrics.name: Bézout's theorem (Theorem 80.4.5)
rubrics_metrics.description: Let I be a homogeneous ideal with dim V_pr(I) ≥ 1. If f ∈ C[x0,...,xn] is homogeneous of degree k and does not vanish on any irreducible component of V_pr(I), then deg(I + (f)) = k · deg I. Geometric form: intersecting V with a hypersurface of degree k multiplies the degree by k unless some component is contained in the hypersurface.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof uses exact sequences on graded pieces: 0 → [S/I]_{d−k} → [S/I]_d → [S/(I+(f))]_d → 0; generalizations to schemes handle non-radical ideals. This is the algebraic statement behind classical intersection-degree computations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hypersurface degree corollary (Corollary 80.5.1)
rubrics_metrics.description: If V is a hypersurface with I_rad(V) = (f) and f homogeneous of degree k, then deg V = k.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follows immediately from Bézout's theorem by taking I = (0).

rubrics_metrics.name: Bézout's theorem for plane curves (Corollary 80.5.2)
rubrics_metrics.description: For any two plane curves X and Y in CP^2 without a common irreducible component, |X ∩ Y| ≤ deg X · deg Y (counted with multiplicity).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Classical consequence of Bézout; equality holds under generic transverse intersection conditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of pullback and morphism of baby ringed spaces (Definitions 81.1.2 & 81.1.3)
rubrics_metrics.description: Given baby ringed spaces (X,O_X) and (Y,O_Y) and a continuous map f: X → Y, the pullback f^# of a regular function φ ∈ O_Y(U) is φ ∘ f : f^{-1}(U) → C. The map f is a morphism if every such pullback is a regular function on X (i.e. f^#φ ∈ O_X(f^{-1}(U)) for all φ).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This packages the algebraic condition that regular functions on Y pull back to regular functions on X; equivalently, one obtains for each open U a ring homomorphism f^#: O_Y(U) → O_X(f^{-1}(U)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification of regular maps between affine varieties (Theorem 81.2.2)
rubrics_metrics.description: If X ⊆ A^m and Y ⊆ A^n are affine varieties then every morphism f: X → Y is given globally by polynomials: f(x) = (P_1(x), ..., P_n(x)) where P_i ∈ C[x_1,...,x_m].
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof uses that coordinate projections π_i ∈ O_Y(Y) pull back to elements of O_X(X) = C[X], so each coordinate function is a polynomial; this yields a practical coordinate description of morphisms between affines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regular maps between projective varieties are locally polynomial (Theorem 81.2.4)
rubrics_metrics.description: If X ⊆ CP^m and Y ⊆ CP^n are projective varieties and f: X → Y is a morphism, then for every p ∈ X there exists an open neighborhood U_p and homogeneous polynomials P_0,...,P_n (of the same degree, not all vanishing on U_p) so that f(x) = (P_0(x):...:P_n(x)) for all x ∈ U_p.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Projective morphisms may not be given globally by homogeneous polynomials (example 81.2.3), but they are locally described this way on suitable affine charts; the Pi depend on the neighborhood.

rubrics_metrics.name: Example: projective map not globally polynomial (Example 81.2.3)
rubrics_metrics.description: The map V = V_pr(xy−z^2) ⊆ CP^2 → CP^1 defined piecewise by (x:z) when x ≠ 0 and (z:y) when y ≠ 0 is a morphism but is not given globally by a single tuple of homogeneous polynomials.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This demonstrates the necessity of the 'locally polynomial' formulation for projective morphisms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Isomorphism example V(xy−z^2) ≅ CP^1 (Example 81.2.5)
rubrics_metrics.description: The map CP^1 → V ⊆ CP^2 given by (s:t) ↦ (s^2:t^2:st) is an isomorphism (with inverse given locally), showing the conic V is isomorphic to CP^1.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provides an explicit polynomial parametrization realizing the isomorphism and illustrates how some projective varieties are themselves projective-space-like.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of quasi-projective variety (Definition 81.3.2)
rubrics_metrics.description: A quasi-projective variety is an open subset X of a projective variety V; it is endowed with the induced structure sheaf O_X(U) = O_V(U) for U ⊆ X.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quasi-projective varieties generalize both affine and projective varieties; many affine varieties can be realized as open subsets of projective ones.

rubrics_metrics.name: Every affine is quasi-projective (Proposition 81.3.4)
rubrics_metrics.description: Every affine variety is isomorphic to a quasi-projective one (i.e., to an open subset of some projective variety).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This embeds affine geometry into the projective/quasi-projective framework and underpins many standard compactification/closure arguments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hyperbola effect / Distinguished opens of affines are affine (Theorem 81.4.2)
rubrics_metrics.description: For V = V(f_1,...,f_m) ⊆ A^n and the distinguished open X = D(f) ⊆ V, define W = V(f_1,...,f_m, y·f − 1) ⊆ A^{n+1} where y is the extra coordinate. Then X ≅ W, i.e., distinguished open subsets of affine varieties are affine (the 'hyperbola effect').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Constructs an explicit affine variety W whose coordinate projection realizes the isomorphism; explains why deleting points from A^1 can still yield an affine variety (e.g., A^1 \{0} ≅ V(xy−1)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Pre-sheaf of rings definition (Definition 82.2.2)
rubrics_metrics.description: A pre-sheaf of rings F on a topological space X is an assignment F: OpenSets(X) → Rings sending each open set U to a ring F(U), together with restriction maps res_{U1,U2}: F(U2) → F(U1) for U1 ⊆ U2, satisfying identity and compositional axioms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sections are elements of F(U) and global sections are elements of F(X); think of F(U) as 'functions with property P' on U. There is an equivalent categorical formulation as a contravariant functor OpenSets(X)^{op} → Rings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stalks and germs of a pre-sheaf (Definitions 82.3.1 & 82.3.2)
rubrics_metrics.description: The stalk F_p at a point p is the set of equivalence classes of pairs (s,U) with s ∈ F(U), p ∈ U, where (s1,U1) ∼ (s2,U2) if they agree on some neighborhood V of p; equivalence classes are germs [s]_p.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Germs capture 'enriched local data' around p and stalks are rings under induced operations; germs for analytic or holomorphic sheaves can carry strong reconstruction information (e.g., holomorphic germs determine entire functions by Taylor series).

rubrics_metrics.name: Stalks of the structure sheaf of an affine variety (Theorem 82.3.7)
rubrics_metrics.description: For a variety V ⊆ A^n and a point p ∈ V, the stalk O_{V,p} is isomorphic to the localization {f/g | f,g ∈ C[V], g(p) ≠ 0}, i.e., the local ring of regular functions at p.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This identifies germs of regular functions near p with rational functions regular at p (fractions of coordinate ring elements with denominators nonvanishing at p), making the local ring concrete for computations.
